note: The judges saw only the advisory text and the finding text, with opaque ids and an order fixed by a hash unrelated to the arm. The arm and the original id are joined back in here, afterwards, from a mapping file they never received.

judgements.reason: Describes path traversal: the certificate common name concatenated into dst_path_cn and the filenames, reaching sftp.mkdir/sftp.open on the destination host. The mechanism (untrusted CN in a remote path), the place (lemur_sftp upload/upload_file) and the consequence (arbitrary write/overwrite on the SFTP host) are all different from the advisory's missing authorization and unredacted serialization on the destinations read endpoints.

Names the same secrets the advisory is about (password / privateKeyPass declared as plain str options, stored unencrypted) and even cites the schema serializing the options blob, but the defect it asserts is cleartext storage at rest, with the stated prerequisite being database/backup/dump access. It explicitly defers the HTTP exposure to a separate finding. Same precondition, different mechanism (no encryption at rest vs. read endpoints lacking admin_permission and redaction) and different attacker prerequisite.

A correctness bug in the SFTP plugin's error path: NoValidConnectionsError constructed with a str instead of the mapping paramiko expects, so the handler itself raises AttributeError and the failure is swallowed. Nothing to do with authorization on the destinations API or with serialization of option values.

Points at CertificateDestinations.get, one of the unguarded read routes, but the defect asserted is a schema-arity mismatch (singular destination_output_schema decorating a handler that calls the paginated service.render), whose worst case it frames as a crash in fill_object. Same file and same handler, different mechanism (decorator arity) and different consequence (broken/redundant response, not credential disclosure); it makes no claim about authorization or redaction.

Swallowed exceptions in upload_file/delete_file (re-raise nested inside `if hasattr(e, 'errors')`), so a failed deployment is recorded as success. Availability/integrity-of-state defect in the SFTP plugin, not the advisory's disclosure of stored option values through the destinations read endpoints.

RejectPolicy installed with no known_hosts ever loaded, so every SFTP connection fails closed at host-key verification. A connectivity/fail-closed defect in the plugin; different mechanism, different place and no credential disclosure.

Exactly the advisory's defect: DestinationOutputSchema declares options as an unallowlisted, unredacted list of dicts and fill_object copies the stored option values (including the SFTP password and privateKeyPass) into the response, while DestinationsList.get / Destinations.get / CertificateDestinations.get carry only validate_schema on AuthenticatedResource where post/put/delete carry admin_permission.require(403). Same mechanism, same place, same consequence (any authenticated, including read-only, user obtains the destination credentials).

Unconditional sftp.chmod(..., 0o644) applied to the uploaded .key file, leaving the private key world-readable on the destination host. Different mechanism (file permissions on the remote host) and a different consequence (local disclosure of the deployed key) from the advisory's API-level exposure of destination credentials.

Same swallowed-exception defect in upload_file/delete_file as P-017: failures without an `.errors` attribute are logged and discarded so the caller records success. Silent non-delivery, not the destinations read endpoints' missing authorization/redaction.

Lands on the exact hook the advisory blames for leaking the options (fill_object in DestinationOutputSchema), but the defect asserted is unguarded key/index access on malformed stored option shapes, whose consequence is a 500 across the whole destinations listing. Same place, different mechanism (missing guards vs. missing redaction/authorization) and a denial-of-service consequence instead of credential disclosure.

Same hook as the advisory (fill_object, schemas.py:33-36) and it even quotes the line that copies the options into the response, but what it calls the defect is the unguarded option["type"]/option["value"] indexing that lets one malformed row break the listing for everyone. Different mechanism and consequence (availability of the endpoint, not disclosure of the credentials it returns).

Path traversal through the certificate common name into dst_path_cn and the .key/.pem filenames, with recursive sftp.mkdir and a PermissionError-driven chmod-then-overwrite. Different mechanism, different place and a remote-filesystem write consequence, not the destinations API disclosure.

Same module and the same broad theme of an authenticated-only destinations read handler with no admin gate, but it targets DestinationsStats.get (views.py:434) and the mechanism it names is a missing @validate_schema plus an unvalidated `metric` reqparse argument splatted into service.stats. Different endpoint, different mechanism, and the payload it worries about is not the credential-bearing plugin options.

The advisory's defect stated directly: the three destination read handlers carry only validate_schema on AuthenticatedResource while post/put/delete carry admin_permission.require(403), and DestinationOutputSchema/fill_object return the stored option values unredacted, so any authenticated (including read-only) user reads the plaintext SFTP password and privateKeyPass. Same mechanism, same place, same consequence.

Identifies the per-method authorization asymmetry in lemur/destinations/views.py (writes gated by admin_permission, reads only login-required via AuthenticatedResource) combined with the unredacted options list in DestinationOutputSchema.fill_object, yielding cleartext SFTP password and key passphrase to any session holder. Same mechanism, same place, same consequence as the advisory.

The upload_file/delete_file swallowed-exception defect again: the re-raise is nested under `hasattr(e, 'errors')` so failed deliveries return normally and stale certificates stay in place. Different mechanism, different place and a state-integrity consequence, not the credential disclosure the advisory describes.

Unconditional chmod 0o644 on every uploaded file including the .key, exposing the deployed private key to any local account on the destination host. A file-permission defect on the remote host; different mechanism and different consequence from the destinations API returning stored credentials.

Path traversal via the certificate common name reaching dst_path_cn, the filename stems, sftp.mkdir-walk, sftp.open and chmod, letting a certificate requester choose where on the destination host files land. Different mechanism, different place, different consequence from the advisory's unauthorized read of destination plugin credentials.

CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION hook skipped on the upload path when `destinations` is set (early return at views.py:657). Different mechanism (config-hook ordering bug) and different consequence (site policy bypass) from the advisory's unchecked `replaces[]` ORM resolution and notification/rotation hijack.

Export authorization nested inside `if plugin.requires_key:` while the private key is passed to the plugin regardless. A private-key disclosure via the export route, unrelated to the `replaces[]` array or to notify/replaced state.
Bare `raise Exception` for a missing private key producing a 500 instead of a 4xx. Error-handling defect, no relation to the unchecked replacement references.

Domain authorization evaluated on `common_name`/`extensions` while a caller-supplied CSR is signed verbatim (service.py:451). Unauthorized issuance for arbitrary names - a different input, a different check and a different consequence than the unchecked `replaces[]` list.
Missing audit-log entry on the export route. Logging/forensics gap, not the missing ownership/CertificatePermission check on referenced certificates.
Raw exception text echoed in stats/revoke/deactivate responses. Information disclosure through error strings, unrelated to replacement handling.
Same raw-exception-echo defect as reported elsewhere (views.py:690/1708/1775). Information leak via error messages, not the `replaces[]` authorization gap.

Authorization reads `common_name`/`extensions` while `service.mint` signs the caller's CSR (service.py:447). Unauthorized CA issuance via CSR substitution - a distinct mechanism from resolving attacker-named certificates into `Certificate.replaces`.

Security-relevant preconditions written as bare `assert` statements strippable under `python -O`. Robustness defect in get_certificate_primitives/get_all_valid_certs, not the missing permission check on `replaces[]`.

CERTIFICATE_EXPORT_KEY_REQUEST_VALIDATION hook applied on /certificates/<id>/key but not on /certificates/<id>/export. A key-egress policy-hook asymmetry; different route, different control, different consequence.
`terms[1]` indexed without checking the split shape in service.render, producing an IndexError/500. Availability/input-validation bug in the listing filter, unrelated to the advisory.

Upload path omits the `is_valid_owner` check that the create path enforces, allowing an arbitrary owner attribution. Different missing validation (owner field) with a different consequence from the unchecked replacement references.
`validate_no_duplicate_destinations` not reached from CertificatesUpload.post. Missing destination-collision guard; different field, different mechanism, different consequence.

CertificatePermission check nested under the caller-chosen `plugin.requires_key` flag while `cert.private_key` is passed to the plugin unconditionally. Private-key disclosure on the export route, not the `replaces[]` ownership gap.

Missing None check on `service.get(certificate_id).replaces` at views.py:1494, yielding a 500 instead of a 404. It touches the `replaces` relationship only as a read on a different route; the defect is an unguarded dereference, not the absence of a CertificatePermission check when `replaces[]` is written on create/upload/update.
A Role object appended to a list of role names, so AuthorityPermission never matches - a fail-closed correctness bug in the authority grant. Different code, different (non-exposure) consequence.
No `log_service.create` entry on the upload handler. Missing audit trail for uploads; no relation to replacement resolution or notification suppression.
`allowed_issuance_for_domain` authorizes only x509.DNSName SANs while create_csr adds every SAN type. Unauthorized issuance for non-DNS identifiers - a different check on a different input.
Soft-deleted certificates still readable by id/name including the private key, because only the list query honours the `deleted` flag. Different mechanism (missing filter predicate) and consequence.

ROTATE_AUTHORITY_TRANSLATION can set `primitives['authority']` to None, crashing rotation. Rotation is mentioned, but the defect is an unchecked authority lookup causing an AttributeError outage, not certificate hijack through unchecked `replaces[]`.
`conditions` dict mutated while iterating its own keys in get_by_attributes, raising RuntimeError. Sanitiser correctness bug unrelated to the advisory.
Optional `filter` parameter dereferenced and indexed without validation, raising AttributeError/IndexError. Input-validation/500 defect on read endpoints, not the replacement-authorization gap.

`g.current_user != cert.user` short-circuits every CertificatePermission gate, so the original creator keeps key/update access after ownership transfer. Missing-authorization family, but a different mechanism (creator exemption on key/update/revoke routes) and a different consequence from the unchecked `replaces[]` array on create/upload/update.
No `export_private_key` audit record on the plugin export route. Detection/forensics gap on key egress, not the advisory's missing permission check on referenced certificates.
`calculate_reissue_range` truncates to whole days and treats max_issuance_days == 0 as no maximum. Validity-cap arithmetic defect, unrelated to `replaces[]`.
Malformed `filter`/`serial` query parameters produce unhandled 500s. Input-validation/error-noise defect on read routes, not the advisory's authorization gap.
Same unvalidated `filter` parsing on /certificates/valid raising AttributeError/IndexError. Availability/error-handling defect, unrelated to replacement handling.

CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION hook unreachable on upload when a destination is supplied. Deployment policy-hook bypass via branch ordering; different mechanism and consequence from unchecked `replaces[]`.
Only DNSName SANs passed to `is_authorized_for_domain`; IP/URI/email/otherName SANs reach the CSR unchecked. Unauthorized issuance for non-DNS identifiers - a different input and a different check.

Domain authorization skipped entirely when `authority.is_private_authority` is set (views.py:538). Issuance-authorization gap scoped to the CA flag, not the ownership check missing on the `replaces[]` references.

allowed_issuance_for_domain calls is_authorized_for_domain only under `isinstance(san, x509.DNSName)`. Same SAN-type gap as the other issuance findings; a different defect from the unchecked replacement array.

Export handler's only CertificatePermission check sits inside the `plugin.requires_key` branch while `cert.private_key` is passed to the plugin unconditionally. Missing authorization, but on the export route and keyed off a caller-selected plugin flag - not the resolution of `replaces[]` into Certificate objects.
Export passphrase written into the shared plugin singleton's `options` and not scrubbed on exception. Cross-request secret leakage through process-wide plugin state; unrelated to the advisory.

Upload returns at views.py:657 before the CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION hook whenever destinations are supplied. Policy-hook bypass via branch ordering, not the unchecked `replaces[]` ownership gap.

`service.get(certificate_id).replaces` dereferenced without a None check, returning 500 instead of 404 and acting as an existence oracle. Touches the replaces relationship only as a read; the mechanism (missing null guard) and consequence (500/oracle) are not the advisory's missing CertificatePermission check on written replacements.

Lands in the advisory's affected route (CertificatesUpload.post) but the mechanism is an early return past the optional CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION hook when `destinations` is set. The advisory's upload defect is that the handler accepts attacker-supplied `body`/`authority`/`external_id` with no AuthorityPermission check and no uniqueness constraint, enabling a duplicate row that revoke then honours at the CA. Same handler, different missing control, different consequence (site policy skipped, not CA-side revocation of a third party's certificate).

Different route and different defect: POST /certificates/<id>/export nests the CertificatePermission check inside `if plugin.requires_key` while passing cert.private_key to the plugin regardless. That is private-key disclosure via a caller-chosen plugin flag; the advisory is about duplicate-row upload plus row-scoped revoke authorization causing CA-side revocation.

Same handler as the advisory's upload route (views.py:659) but the defect described is a bare `raise Exception` used for input validation, producing a 500 instead of a 4xx. No authorization, no duplicate row, no revocation - only co-location with the advisory's route.

Different defect: service.mint signs a caller-supplied CSR while allowed_issuance_for_domain authorized the separate common_name/extensions fields, yielding unauthorized issuance for names the caller does not control. The advisory is about revoking an existing certificate at the CA via a duplicate uploaded row, not about what gets signed.

Missing audit_log record on the export route. Different route, different mechanism (logging gap), different consequence (forensic blindness) from the advisory's upload-duplicate-then-revoke authorization bypass.

Verbatim `str(e)` echoed from the stats, revoke and deactivate handlers. The primary locus is the stats handler and the mechanism is error-message information disclosure; the revoke handler appears only as one instance of that pattern, not as the advisory's row-scoped authorization defect.

Same error-text reflection pattern as P-015, headed at views.py:690 (stats). Information disclosure via exception strings is neither the advisory's mechanism (duplicate Certificate row + creator/row-scoped revoke authorization) nor its consequence (CA-side revocation of another party's certificate).

Same defect as P-010 - authorization reads common_name/extensions while issuance signs the caller's own CSR. Unauthorized issuance, not revocation of an existing certificate at the CA; different mechanism and different consequence from the advisory.
Bare `assert` statements removed under python -O in get_certificate_primitives and get_all_valid_certs. Unrelated to upload authorization or to how revoke authorizes the caller.

CERTIFICATE_EXPORT_KEY_REQUEST_VALIDATION applied on GET /certificates/<id>/key but not on POST /certificates/<id>/export. A key-egress hook asymmetry on the export route; different route, mechanism and consequence from the advisory's revoke-by-duplicate-upload.

Unchecked `terms[1]` after splitting the `filter` argument in service.render, an IndexError-driven 500. Availability nuisance on a listing route, unrelated to certificate upload or revoke authorization.

Correctly identifies that CertificatesUpload.post skips a validation the create route enforces, and it is the advisory's affected route - but the missing check it names is is_valid_owner, and the consequence is misattributed ownership/notification routing. The advisory's upload gap is the absent AuthorityPermission check and the absence of uniqueness on body/serial/external_id, which is what makes the duplicate row revocable at the CA. Same route, different missing control, different consequence.

Same route as the advisory (upload calling service.upload without validate_no_duplicate_destinations), but the duplication it concerns is two destinations resolving to the same plugin/account, causing one certificate to overwrite another downstream. The advisory's duplication is a duplicate Certificate row carrying another party's body/external_id, and its consequence is CA-side revocation. Different mechanism, different consequence.

Export-route authorization gated on the caller-selected plugin's requires_key flag while the private key is passed to plugin.export unconditionally. Private-key disclosure on POST /certificates/<id>/export, not the advisory's upload-duplicate plus row-scoped revoke path.
Missing None check on service.get in the replacements handler, producing a 500 instead of a 404. Robustness defect on an unrelated route.

AuthorityPermission built from a list mixing a Role object with role-name strings on the creation route, so the authority-owner grant never matches. It fails closed (legitimate users denied), the opposite consequence to the advisory, and it is on the issuance route rather than upload or revoke.

In the advisory's affected route: CertificatesUpload.post returns without calling log_service.create. But the defect asserted is a missing audit record for uploads; the advisory's defect is that the same handler accepts attacker-controlled body/authority/external_id with no AuthorityPermission or uniqueness check, and that revoke then trusts the resulting row. Same handler, different mechanism and consequence (no attribution trail, not certificate revocation at the CA).

allowed_issuance_for_domain authorizing only x509.DNSName SANs while create_csr adds every SAN type. That is unauthorized issuance for non-DNS identifiers - a different defect from revoking an existing certificate through a duplicate uploaded row.

Soft deletion honoured only by the list query, so deleted certificates and their keys stay readable by id/name. Different mechanism (missing `deleted` predicate on read paths) and different consequence (stale read access) from the advisory.

ROTATE_AUTHORITY_TRANSLATION resolving to a non-existent authority id sets primitives['authority'] to None and crashes auto-rotation. A rotation availability bug, unrelated to upload or revoke authorization.

get_by_attributes pops keys from the dict it is iterating, raising RuntimeError depending on insertion order. Implementation defect in a query helper, not the advisory's authorization/duplicate-row mechanism.

Unvalidated `filter` parsing on /certificates/valid and related query-parameter parsing raising unhandled exceptions. Error-handling defect on read routes; the finding explicitly claims no attacker gain beyond an error response.

The closest of the set: it names the exact short-circuit the advisory depends on - `if g.current_user != cert.user` in front of every CertificatePermission check, including the revoke gate - and notes that cert.user is never rewritten. But it frames the exploit as a former creator retaining access after an ownership transfer, and the consequence as continued key export/update/revoke over a certificate that user really did create. It never reaches the advisory's mechanism: manufacturing creator status by uploading a duplicate row carrying another party's body/authority/external_id, so that revoke acts at the CA on the real production certificate. Part of the advisory's chain, not the defect.
No export_private_key audit record on the export route. Logging gap on a different route; the advisory concerns authorization at revoke and validation at upload.
calculate_reissue_range truncating to whole days and treating max_issuance_days == 0 as unlimited. Validity-window defect in reissue, unrelated to upload or revocation authorization.
Malformed `filter` and `serial` query parameters producing unhandled 500s. Input-validation robustness on read endpoints, not the advisory's mechanism or consequence.
Same /certificates/valid filter parsing crash as P-063/P-055. Unrelated route and defect.

Same finding as P-003: the destinations branch returns before CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION, so an operator-installed policy hook can be skipped on upload. It is the advisory's route, but the bypassed control is an optional deployment hook, not the AuthorityPermission/uniqueness gap, and the consequence stops at accepting a policy-violating certificate rather than revoking a third party's certificate at the CA.

DNSName-only authorization in allowed_issuance_for_domain letting IP/URI/RFC822 SANs be signed unchecked. Unauthorized issuance of identifiers, a different defect from revoking an existing certificate via a duplicate row.

allowed_issuance_for_domain skipped entirely when authority.is_private_authority is set, so any name can be minted from a private CA. Issuance authorization on the create route, not the upload/revoke chain the advisory describes.

Full walkthrough of allowed_issuance_for_domain checking only x509.DNSName entries. Same class as P-044/P-070 - unauthorized issuance of non-DNS identifiers - not the advisory's duplicate-upload-then-revoke defect.

CertificateExport.post running its only CertificatePermission check inside the `if plugin.requires_key` branch while cert.private_key is handed to the plugin regardless. Missing authorization on the export route with key-disclosure consequence; the advisory's missing authorization is on revoke, scoped to the DB row rather than the CA-side identity, with revocation as the consequence.
Export passphrase written into the shared plugin singleton's options and scrubbed without try/finally. Secret-lifetime/concurrency defect on the export route, unrelated to the advisory.

Third statement of the same upload hook bypass (early return at views.py:657 ahead of CERTIFICATE_CREATE_REQUEST_VALIDATION at 662). The advisory's route, but a different missing control and a different consequence: site policy skipped on entry, not revocation of another party's certificate at the CA through a duplicate row.
service.get(certificate_id).replaces dereferenced without a None check, returning 500 rather than 404. Robustness/existence-oracle defect on an unrelated route.
